column1: # Sumner's DISCLOSED editorial interventions in the 1825 text.
# WHAT THIS IS: every place where Sumner himself, in a footnote, tells the reader that what he
# printed differs from the manuscript. These are his own admissions, harvested from the plates as
# the volume run reads them. Primary evidence, free, and not anticipated by PLAN §6.4, which
# listed only Campbell/Corns/Hale/Tweedie and the 1825 facsimile plates as sources.
# WHAT THIS IS NOT: a list of everywhere the 1825 departs from SP 9/61. Sumner normalised
# silently and at scale (PLAN §4a). This file records only what he ADMITTED. Never present it as
# a complete collation — the undisclosed changes are the larger and more dangerous set.
# Ruled 2026-08-04 (Wilson): harvest as we go; feeds PLAN §6.4 at M4.
# SCOPE RULED 2026-08-04 (Wilson), CONVENTIONS §5a: this file holds TEXTUAL notes only — the ones
# where Sumner admits the manuscript differs from what he printed, or that he changed something.
# SCHOLARLY Latin notes (Sumner assembling authorities, glossing an allusion, defending Milton)
# are transcribed in the chunk's ## apparatus-sumner-la and get NO row here. When in doubt, do not
# ledger it. This file answers exactly one question — where did Sumner admit changing the text? —
# and a page of Reformed proof-texts filed as an "intervention" would corrupt that answer.
# Deliberately NOT ledgered so far:
#   II.vii, La p. 454, [^la4] — scholarly. Bucer/Calvin/Ursinus/Gomarus for Milton on the Sabbath,
#   Peter Martyr against, Musculus last. Hinge: 'Omnes hactenus cum Miltono faciunt.'
# LAYER COLUMN ADDED 2026-08-28, from I.ii. The file was built assuming textual notes are a
# Latin-volume phenomenon and its page column was called `la_page`. En 20's note 7 disproves that:
# it is a textual note printed in the ENGLISH volume, where Sumner says the manuscript's next
# clause was "incorrectly transcribed" and states what he rendered instead. The truer rule is that
# Sumner puts a textual note wherever his reader needs it — in the Latin volume when the Latin is
# doubtful, in the English when the doubt changed his translation. `layer` is `la` or `en-sumner`
# and `page` is that volume's printed page. CONVENTIONS §5a's two-kind classification is unchanged;
# only the assumption about which volume carries such notes was wrong.
# kind vocabulary (extend as needed, don't invent synonyms):
#   word-order   Sumner rearranged Milton's words
#   emendation   Sumner changed a reading
#   supplement   Sumner supplied something absent from the MS
#   ms-state     Sumner reports damage, a gap, or a hand-change without changing the text
#   uncertain    Sumner flags the MS reading as doubtful
#   ms-error     Sumner says the MS reading is a slip and states the correct one, but prints the slip
#                unchanged (added 2026-09-29, I.xix La 250: "Sic ex incuria scriptum. Oportuit qui")

column7: MS word order differs from the printed text; Sumner reordered the clause about Matt. v. 33 / Jacob. v. 12 so that "per Deum jurare non prohibemur" follows the Matthew citation rather than the James one.
column8: Quo melius ratio grammatica servaretur, ordinem leviter mutavi — to preserve the grammar.

column7: Sumner flags the MS reading `qualis ipse est` as doubtful and asks whether `se` should be read — i.e. whether Milton wrote that God wills to be conceived as he IS, or as he PRESENTS HIMSELF. The text is printed unchanged.
column8: Sic in MS. An legendum se? — the MS reads thus; query the reading.

column7: Sumner flags `SUMME BEATUS` (most blessed) as the MS reading and asks whether `benignus` (most gracious) should be read, on the ground of the context and the texts cited. The Latin is printed unchanged — but he then TRANSLATED the emendation: En 28 reads "He is MOST GRACIOUS", with no English note. Printed the MS in one layer, adopted the conjecture in the other.
column8: Sic in MS. Sed vide an legendum benignus, quod et contextus, et loci citati postulare videntur — context and the cited passages seem to require it.

column7: The ledger's FIRST English-volume row. On Exod. iii. 14 Sumner quotes the manuscript verbatim, judges the clause after `Ehie qui sum vel ero` to have been incorrectly transcribed, and states the reconstruction he translated from (`et si persona prima in tertiam affinis verbi mutatur, Jave, qui est vel erit`), citing Simon's Hebrew Lexicon, Buxtorf and Cappellus. The Latin volume prints the MS clause with no note at all, so this admission exists in the English layer only.
column8: conceiving the next clause to have been incorrectly transcribed, I have rendered it as if it had been written—

column7: Sumner flags `insontes non minus justum fuit … multare` as contrary to the argument, which seems to require `magis justum` or `minus injustum`; he says the same adverb errs again in Cap. 31. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 263) silently renders the sense he proposes (`as unjust`).
column8: Argumenti ratio poscere videtur aut magis justum, aut minus injustum. Eodem adverbio peccatur infra Cap. 31. — the argument seems to require the other reading.

column7: In the English text of I.xiii Sumner prints Euripides, Suppl. 532-534, with Porson's `φῶς` for `σῶμ'` and Gataker's `ἀπελθεῖν` for `ἀπῆλθε`. The Latin volume (La 199) prints the lines as Milton quoted them, `σῶμ'` and `ἀπῆλθε`, and its own note gives only the line reference. The change is to a quotation, not to Milton's words, and the admission is partial: Sumner names the old readings but never says they are the ones Milton wrote. Ruled into scope 2026-09-25 (Wilson).
column8: This is the reading proposed by Porson … In the next line the old reading was ἀπῆλθε. Gataker proposed ἀπελθεῖν, which emendation was adopted by Musgrave, and approved by Porson. — no reason given beyond the editors' authority.

column7: Sumner flags the construction `adiri Deus, tolli peccatum, lex adimpleri, ira Dei, potestas Satanæ, morsque … sustineri ac vinci` as labouring, and says the accusative is required here and in what follows. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 303–304) renders the accusative sense with active verbs: `none but God is able to approach God, to take away sin, to fulfil the law …`.
column8: Constructio plane laborat. Hic et in sequentibus quartus casus requiritur. — the construction plainly labours; the accusative is required.

column7: Sumner queries `duplexque in eo intellectus, duplex voluntas maneat` and proposes `ne` for `que` (duplexne, 'whether twofold'). The text is printed unchanged, and as printed it asserts the twofold intellect and will. The English (En 304) silently follows the conjecture: `whether he retains his two-fold will and understanding, is a point respecting which … we are not concerned to inquire`.
column8: An legendum ne? — should ne be read?

column7: Sumner says `sensus ille divinæ misericordiæ, quæ ad resipiscentiam ducit, non est cum fide confundenda` was written carelessly: the relative and the gerundive should agree with `sensus`, not `misericordiæ` (`qui … confundendus`). The text is printed unchanged, with the slip. The English (En 350) silently follows the correction: `that sense of the divine mercy, which leads to repentance, ought not to be confounded with faith`.
column8: Sic ex incuria scriptum. Oportuit qui, et mox confundendus. — written thus through carelessness; it should have been qui, and then confundendus.

column7: Sumner suggests `declaret` for the printed `declararet` (La ¶18, `ut illius sententiæ justitiam eo manifestius universis hominibus declararet`), to keep the sequence of tenses after the present `ferre`. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 377) renders the present-tense sense: `that he may thereby make the equity of his judgement manifest to all mankind`.
column8: Præferat aliquis declaret, ut temporum ratio melius servetur. — someone may prefer declaret, so that the sequence of tenses is better kept.

column7: Sumner reconstructs a correction history in the MS at the definition of a sacrament (La ¶5): the amanuensis first wrote `obedientiam nostram grata recordatione testamur`; Milton had `sincero animi proposito` interlined, then wanted `proposito` struck, intending `sincero animo et grata recordatione`. The scribe changed `animi` to `animo` but left `proposito` standing. The page imitates the MS (`sincero ani` + a printed blot + `·mo` interlined). The text is printed with the leftover word (`sincero animo proposito et grata recordatione`). The English (En 429) follows the intended reading: `with a sincere heart and a grateful remembrance`.
column8: Quisquis is fuerit, cujus calamum in opere scribendo auctor jam cæcus mutuum acceperit — whoever it was whose pen the author, now blind, borrowed in writing the work.

column7: Sumner says the sense of `quanto minus ab evangelica vis omnis et coactio remotissima esse debet?` (La ¶14) requires `magis`, and refers back to his note at La p. 181 (I.xi `[^la8]`, which had flagged the same adverb going wrong in Cap. 31). The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 486–487) silently follows the correction: `how much more ought the gratitude which we owe for the benefits of the gospel to be exempt from the slightest shadow of force or constraint?`
column8: Sensus loci magis postulat. Vide quæ notata sunt supra p. 181. — the sense of the passage requires magis; see what was noted above at p. 181.

column7: At Jacob. i. 18 (I.iv La ¶13) Sumner reports the MS reading `quia voluit: nempe in Christo. Qui scilicet sermo, illi et veritas est, progenuit nos sermone veritatis.` and proposes repunctuating it as a parenthesis. The Latin text is printed unchanged. The English (En 50) silently translates the repunctuated text: `of his own will,—that is, in Christ, who is the word and truth of God,—begat he us with the word of truth.`
column8: Sic in MS. An legendum, mutata tantum interpunctione, quia voluit—, nempe in Christo, qui scilicet sermo illi et veritas est,—progenuit nos &c.? — so in the MS; should it be read, changing only the punctuation, …?

column7: In I.iv part b (La ¶2, La 41) the Latin prints `Qui igitur dilecti dilecturi erant, id est, credituri, eos prænovit Deus` with no Latin note. Sumner's English note quotes the clause, says it scarcely makes sense unless it alludes to John xvi. 27, and judges `dilecti` more probably a transcriber's insertion. The English text translates without it: `Those therefore who were about to love, that is, to believe in God, God foreknew or approved`. As at I.ii [^s7], the admission exists in the English layer only.
column8: It seems more probable that dilecti has been inserted by the carelessness of the transcriber.

column7: In the Præfatio (I.v-a La ¶1) the Latin prints `id libere expromo, quod multo mihi … liquere clarius ex sacris literis videtur` and Sumner's note says the MS reading is a slip and the sense requires `expromam`. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 80) has no note here, and `freely advance` does not show which reading it translates.
column8: Ita scriptum, incuria ut videtur; sensus enim postulat expromam. — so written, apparently by carelessness; for the sense requires expromam.

column7: In the Præfatio (I.v-a La ¶1, La 57) the Latin prints `quid est æquius quam ut permittant alteri eandem atque ipsi ratione ac via veritatem indaganti` with no Latin note. Sumner's English note quotes the clause and calls `eandem` probably an error for `eadem`. The English text translates the corrected ablative: `who is seeking truth through the same means and in the same way as themselves`. As at I.iv-b [^s5], the admission exists in the English layer only.
column8: The sentence is thus written in the original … probably an error for eadem.

column7: In I.v-b La ¶7 the Latin prints `si natura necessario egit, Patrem sibi natura gignendo se imminuit` and Sumner asks whether `parem` should be read. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 86) silently translates the conjecture: `the Father impaired himself by physically begetting a co-equal`.
column8: Sic in MS. An parem? — so in the MS; should it be parem?

column7: In I.v-b La ¶10 the Latin prints `hoc enim nos est gignere sed repugnantia loqui` and Sumner suggests `non` for `nos`. The text is printed unchanged. The English (En 87–88) silently translates the conjecture: `which would be a contradiction of terms instead of a mode of generation`.
column8: Forte rectius non. — perhaps non is more correct.
